query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin aluminide coating to the surface of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr will form a continuous, protective Al2O3 scale at elevated temperatures, thereby significantly improving its oxygen resistance without degrading its room- and high-temperature mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, but with inadequate resistance to oxidation (pesting) in air.
generation.intervention: Surface aluminizing treatment via pack cementation to deposit a thin aluminide coating.
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at 800 °C for 5 hours; mechanical property evaluations at room temperature and near 1000 °C; low to moderate mechanical loading during oxidation exposure.
generation.structural_mediator: A dense, adherent Al2O3 (alumina) scale formed on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: The aluminide coating reacts with oxygen during high-temperature exposure to form a continuous, slow-growing alumina layer that acts as an effective barrier to oxygen diffusion, thereby mitigating oxidation (pesting) without altering the bulk microstructure that governs mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy will exhibit significantly reduced oxygen uptake and oxide scale growth (improved oxidation resistance) while maintaining its characteristic room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength, compared to the untreated alloy.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr oxidizes rapidly in air at high temperatures, leading to pesting and degradation of mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: Applicability limited to conditions up to 800 °C in air during a 5-hour exposure with evaluation based on tensile properties at room temperature and near 1000 °C; intervention is intended for as-cast alloys without additional thermomechanical processing.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in oxidation resistance and any minor effects of the coating process on mechanical properties remain to be determined via systematic experimentation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples: one set will receive a thin aluminide coating via pack cementation, while the other set will remain untreated. Subject both sets to air exposure at 800 °C for 5 hours. After exposure, measure weight gain, examine the oxide scale characteristics with microscopy, and perform tensile tests at room temperature and near 1000 °C to assess ductility and yield strength.
measurements: Weight gain per surface area (to quantify oxidation rate)
Oxide scale thickness and continuity (via microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated specimens do not show a statistically significant reduction (e.g., >20% lower weight gain and thinner, more continuous oxide scale) compared to untreated specimens, or if the mechanical properties (ductility or yield strength) deteriorate by more than 10% relative to the untreated alloy, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

A Promising New Class of High-Temperature Alloys: Eutectic High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

Effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on Mechanical Properties of Equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr Alloys

Abstract: AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Tuning Microstructure and Mechanical Performance of a Co-Rich Transformation-Induced Plasticity High Entropy Alloy

Abstract: AbstractMulti-principal element alloys and high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are emerging metallic materials with unprecedented structures and properties for various applications. In this study, we tuned the microstructure and mechanical performance of a recently designed high-performance Co-rich TRIP-HEA via thermomechanical processing (TMP). The microstructures of the HEA after various TMP routines were characterized, and their correlation with room-temperature tensile performance was clarified. The results showed that grain refinement is an effective strategy for enhancing strength while retaining satisfactory ductility. The formation of incoherent precipitates slightly improves the strength but inevitably sacrifices the ductility, which needs to be considered for optimizing the TMPs.
